definition: H2O is an open-source, in-memory, distributed machine learning and predictive analytics platform developed by the company H2O.ai (previously 0xdata).
details: The software uses a distributed architecture for parallel processing on standard hardware. It supports algorithms for large-scale data analysis and model deployment. H2O is primarily used by data scientists and developers for statistical modeling and data-driven decision-making. The platform is designed to handle in-memory computations across a distributed computing environment. It offers implementations for numerous statistical and machine learning algorithms, which are accessible through various programming interfaces. The software is released under the Apache License 2.0.

explainer.lead: H2O is an open-source platform for training and deploying machine-learning models across multiple computers. It matters because it lets data science teams apply statistical and machine-learning algorithms to large datasets using distributed, in-memory computation on standard hardware.

tiers.eli5: H2O is like asking a group of computers to solve parts of the same big puzzle at once, then putting their answers together. It helps people learn patterns from data and use those patterns to make predictions. The computers keep the information close at hand while working, rather than passing every task to just one machine.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers and data scientists use H2O through its programming interfaces to run statistical and machine-learning algorithms in a distributed computing environment. Models can then be used in deployment workflows for prediction and data-driven decision-making. Because computation is in memory, cluster memory and workload size need to be planned together; distributed execution does not remove the need to choose and evaluate an appropriate algorithm.
tiers.paperLevel: H2O is a distributed in-memory machine-learning platform: a dataset and its intermediate computations are processed across a computing environment, with algorithms executing in parallel on standard hardware. It provides a common platform for multiple statistical and machine-learning methods rather than defining one estimator or objective function. Its scaling and predictive performance therefore depend on the selected algorithm, data, and computing environment.

explainer.example: A data science team could spread a large dataset across several standard machines, use H2O to train a statistical model with distributed in-memory computation, and then deploy the resulting model to generate predictions for new records.

explainer.intuition: Instead of making one computer handle an entire modeling job, H2O spreads the work across a distributed environment and keeps computation in memory. The same platform exposes many statistical and machine-learning algorithms through programming interfaces.
howItWorks: A data science workload is brought into H2O's distributed computing environment.
The platform performs in-memory computation across the available machines.
Its statistical or machine-learning algorithms process the workload in parallel on standard hardware.
The resulting model can support predictions and model deployment.
explainer.whyItMatters: H2O combines large-scale distributed processing, multiple modeling algorithms, programming interfaces, and deployment support in one open-source platform. Its Apache License 2.0 release makes the software openly available to data scientists and developers.
misconceptions: H2O is not a single machine-learning algorithm; it is a platform that implements many algorithms.
Distributed, in-memory processing does not guarantee better predictive accuracy.
H2O is the software platform, while H2O.ai, previously 0xdata, is the company that developed it.
